issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction based on circumstantial evidence can be sustained when the inference of guilt is not the only possible inference that can be drawn from the facts.

law.fact_text: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which guilt is inferred must first be fully established.
law.law_text: The established circumstances must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused.

law.fact_text: The circumstances should be of such a nature as to reasonably exclude every hypothesis except the one of guilt.
law.law_text: The chain of evidence must be so complete that it leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.

law.fact_text: Circumstantial evidence is defined as a combination of facts that, when taken as a whole, do not admit of any inference other than the accused's guilt.
law.law_text: For a conviction to be sustained on circumstantial evidence, the inference of guilt must be the only reasonable inference possible from the evidence.

application.fact_text: The court considered the issue of whether a conviction can be sustained when the evidence allows for inferences other than guilt.
application.law_text: The court applied the established legal standard that circumstantial evidence must point exclusively to the guilt of the accused.

application.fact_text: The court reiterated that the evidence must "reasonably exclude every hypothesis but the one proposed to be proved."
application.law_text: This means that if the facts can support a reasonable conclusion consistent with innocence, the standard for conviction has not been met.

application.fact_text: The court emphasized that the chain of evidence must be complete, creating a network through which there is "no escape for the accused" because the facts "do not admit of any inference but of his guilt."
application.law_text: Therefore, the existence of another possible and reasonable inference drawn from the facts is fatal to the prosecution's case.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that a conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot be sustained if the inference of guilt is not the only possible inference. The court reasoned that the law requires the established facts to be consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt and to exclude every other reasonable hypothesis. If the evidence allows for any reasonable conclusion consistent with innocence, the conviction cannot stand.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a conviction based on circumstantial evidence can be sustained when the inference of guilt is not the only possible inference that can be drawn from the facts.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
The appellants' conduct was inconsistent with guilt, as they were the ones who lodged the FIR and brought the injured person to the hospital for treatment.
The disclosure statements that led to the recovery of the licensed gun and pellets were made by the appellants themselves.
respondent_arguments: The accused-appellants had confessed to their crime.
The confession led to the recovery of incriminating articles, which proves their guilt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met for a conviction: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn must be fully established; (2) the established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused; and (3) the circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and tendency.
obiter: A witness who does not inspire confidence cannot be relied upon.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a case based entirely on circumstantial evidence, a conviction cannot be sustained if an inference other than guilt is possible. For the prosecution to succeed, the inference of guilt must not only be a strong probability but must exist so 'actually and clearly' that it 'completely overcomes all other inferences or hypotheses, as to leave no reasonable doubt of guilt'. The court found that the prosecution failed to meet this standard, as the chain of circumstantial evidence was not complete and did not point exclusively to the guilt of the accused.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established; (2) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; and (3) the circumstances should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty.

When a case is capable of supporting an inference of guilt, but some other inference or theory is also possible, the inference of guilt must completely overcome all other inferences or hypotheses, so as to leave no reasonable doubt of guilt.
In a case wholly dependent on circumstantial evidence, motive forms one of the links in the chain of evidence.
